author: polynoamial
text: @jon_chuang There's a lot of challenges in extending MuZero to imperfect-info games. I think it can be done, but it's not nearly as easy as you describe. For one, predicting the opponent's internal state is insufficient, because then their internal state depends on your internal state, etc.

author: polynoamial
text: The major criticism of AI for games has been that in the real world you don't know the exact model of the interaction. MuZero elegantly and convincingly overcomes this problem (for perfect-info games). In my opinion, it's as significant a breakthrough as AlphaGo and AlphaZero!

quoted.text: In 2016, AlphaGo was introduced. Two years later, its successor - AlphaZero - showed significant progress in Go, chess and shogi. Today in @Nature, our team describes MuZero, a significant step forward in the pursuit of general-purpose algorithms: https://t.co/RVY320HucF https://t.co/gv5wZnGTjn

author: polynoamial
text:
Two major take-aways from this work:
1) External regret minimization, which was behind all the successes in poker, is not limited to purely adversarial games (contrary to what many people believed)
2) As seen in Go, Poker, Hanabi, and now Diplomacy, search makes a huge difference

author: polynoamial
text: @ajoshi944 If the professor indicated a genuine interest in working with you then you should mention them and their research in the statement. But just getting a generic "we can discuss research opportunities if you are admitted" response might not be enough.

author: polynoamial
text: @DIVYANSHJHA The bar is higher if you say in your statement that you want to research deep learning. But if you really do have a strong background in deep learning, then I think it's worth talking about it. You could also list a few related interests with deep learning being one of them.

author: polynoamial
text: @pecey01 This is a good reference that talks about writing research statements: https://t.co/huCalClPLy

author: polynoamial
text: @pecey01 You could always choose to not go there. Being admitted is never a negative.

author: polynoamial
text: @StephenLLH @prantik_deb Yes, I think ideally you'd want to give some details on what kinds of topics within computer vision or game theory you're interested in working on, or what work from a faculty member excited you.

author: polynoamial
text: @dataghees @togelius I haven't served on admissions so I can't really say. For a top program, I think you'd need solid research experience in the area and a strong letter. You should ask your letter writers for their thoughts on how competitive your application is.

author: polynoamial
text: @prantik_deb One option is to make a different research statements for each area. Send the quantum one to schools with quantum faculty and the computer vision one to schools with lots of computer vision faculty. I was interested in both computer vision and game theory, so that's what I did

author: polynoamial
text: Typically, once you're admitted to a program you're not committed to work on what's in your research statement anyway and you can work with any faculty member that's willing to advise you.

author: polynoamial
text: Applying for a PhD in CS/ML? Pro tip: unless you ONLY want to research deep learning or have an amazing background in it, don't emphasize it in your research statement. Lots of strong applications are tossed because they focus on DL and there aren't enough advisors for it.

text: @ctwy I think PhD programs are even more extreme due to how opaque admissions are. For med school or law school you mostly need a good GPA and MCAT/LSAT score. For a top PhD program a 4.0 GPA and perfect GRE isn't enough. You need research experience and letters from the right people.

author: polynoamial
text: This is an under-appreciated problem in academia. A LOT of PhD students at top universities are the children of professors. Why? Because they know how the game is played.

author: polynoamial
text: @ChrKroer @bremen79 @CsabaSzepesvari @bremen79 @ChrKroer, but NormalHedge performs similar to RM in large games, and this is true even when doing things like NormalHedge+ or regret discounting. It's just a more expensive operation. See the NormalHedge section of https://t.co/6cbiMTYGC1

author: polynoamial
text: @ChrKroer @CsabaSzepesvari One explanation is that Hedge requires a tuning parameter while RM is parameter-free. In small games you can tune Hedge to outperform RM, but in large games nobody has found a good way to tune all the parameters automatically. If someone did, it's possible Hedge would be better
